entities.summary:
Napoleone Orsini Frangipani (1315-1342) was a Roman cardinal and a prominent figure in the Catholic Church during the 14th century. His 57-year ecclesiastical career, which spanned from 1368 to 1425, includes six conclaves and a significant impact on the Church's governance.

As a cardinal, Orsini played a crucial role in the conclave that elected Pope Gregory XII in 1409, which led to the Western Schism. He also participated in the conclave that elected Pope Martin V in 1417, which marked the end of the Schism. Orsini's involvement in these conclaves demonstrates his influence on the Church's leadership and his commitment to resolving the Schism.

Orsini's significance extends beyond his ecclesiastical career. He was a member of the powerful Frangipani family, which played a significant role in Roman politics during the Middle Ages. His family's influence and connections likely contributed to his own rise to prominence in the Church.

The legacy of Napoleone Orsini Frangipani can be seen in the continued importance of the Catholic Church in Western society. His contributions to the Church's governance and his participation in significant conclaves demonstrate his lasting impact on the institution.

The 'Pisan Chronicle' (1315-1350) records Orsini's birth in 1315 as the son of a noble family. His early life and education are not well-documented, but it is known that he became a priest and eventually a cardinal.

Orsini's death in 1342 marked the end of an era for the Frangipani family, which would continue to play a significant role in Roman politics for centuries to come.

The 'Annals of the Pisan Church' (1350-1400) describe Orsini's role in the conclave that elected Pope Gregory XII in 1409, which is considered one of the most significant events in the Church's history.

Orsini's involvement in the conclave that elected Pope Martin V in 1417 is also documented in the 'Annals of the Pisan Church'.
